idiom_name: functools.cache (== lru_cache(maxsize=None)) over rule functions keyed by position
implementation_notes: Because a rule is a pure function of the input position, functools.cache is the memo table: the decorator keeps a dictionary keyed by the rule's arguments, stores whatever the function returns - including an explicit failure value - and is documented as thread-safe, with cache_clear() as the escape hatch for the per-input lifecycle. What replaces the classic structure is that the cache lives on the function object rather than in a parser object: no table field, no key construction, no manual hit/miss branch. Two consequences must be respected: lru_cache's default maxsize=128 evicts entries and therefore destroys the linear-time guarantee (use cache, i.e. maxsize=None), and a rule that reads state absent from its arguments gets stale results unless that state is passed in (all arguments must be hashable).
pitfalls: @lru_cache defaults to maxsize=128: eviction silently reintroduces repeated work, so a packrat parser needs cache/maxsize=None (unbounded, per the docs).
The cache is keyed by the arguments only: a rule that reads parser state (indentation, symbol table) must take that state as a hashable argument or it will be answered from a stale entry.
cache keeps references to every argument and result until cache_clear(), and because it hangs off the function object it survives the parse - clear it between inputs or the previous tree stays alive.
Decorating a method caches self as part of the key and keeps instances alive (docs: 'How do I cache method calls?'); prefer module-level rule functions taking the position.
